name: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with CBL mutation
aliases: Noonan syndrome-like disorder with or without juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia

clinicalPearls: Caused by germline variants in CBL, an E3 ubiquitin ligase that normally restrains RAS/MAPK signalling, placing the condition among the RASopathies rather than the chromatin-modifier disorders
The phenotype overlaps Noonan syndrome, with facial dysmorphism, short stature, a broad or webbed neck and variable developmental delay
There is a notable predisposition to juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia (JMML), a myeloproliferative disorder of early childhood
Some CBL-associated JMML behaves indolently and may regress spontaneously, though close haematological monitoring is essential
Cardiac involvement and features overlapping other RASopathies may be present but are often milder than in classic Noonan syndrome
A predisposition to vasculitis and other RAS-pathway-related complications has been described
Diagnosis is molecular, distinguishing germline CBL variants from the somatic CBL changes acquired within leukaemic clones
reference.pathophysiology: CBL encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that tags activated receptor tyrosine kinases for degradation, thereby switching off upstream signals that feed the RAS/MAPK cascade controlling cell growth and proliferation. Loss-of-function or dominant-negative germline variants impair this braking function, so RAS/MAPK signalling remains inappropriately active, a mechanism shared with the wider RASopathy group. The persistent signalling produces the Noonan-like developmental and craniofacial features and, in the haematopoietic compartment, drives the excessive myeloid proliferation that underlies juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia; the same overactivity may contribute to vascular complications, and loss of the remaining normal allele in blood cells can promote clonal expansion.
additionalDifferentials: Noonan syndrome (PTPN11 and other RASopathy genes)
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (with its own JMML risk)
Noonan syndrome-like disorder with loose anagen hair (SHOC2)
Other causes of juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia
additionalInvestigations: Exome or targeted RASopathy panel sequencing to identify germline CBL variants
Full blood count with film and haematology review to screen for myeloproliferation
Bone marrow examination and specialist assessment if JMML is suspected
Growth monitoring and endocrine assessment of short stature
Monitoring for vasculitis and other RAS-pathway complications
redFlags: Hepatosplenomegaly, rising monocytosis or leukocytosis suggesting juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia
Unexplained fever, pallor, bruising or bleeding indicating marrow dysfunction
Features of vasculitis requiring urgent evaluation
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is shaped chiefly by the haematological course: many children do well, and some CBL-associated juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia follows an indolent or self-limiting course, but progressive or aggressive disease can occur and requires specialist haemato-oncology management, so long-term monitoring is essential while developmental and cardiac outcomes are often relatively favourable.
pitfalls: Confusing germline CBL variants with the somatic CBL changes found within leukaemic clones
Assuming all CBL-related juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia is aggressive and over-treating disease that might regress
Overlooking the leukaemia predisposition when the picture is dominated by Noonan-like features
Failing to arrange haematological surveillance after a molecular diagnosis
references: GeneReviews — Noonan Syndrome and related RASopathies (CBL-related disorder)
Nature Reviews Cancer — RAS/MAPK signalling and juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia
management: Undertake close haematological surveillance with full blood count and blood film for juvenile myelomonocytic leukaemia, the key complication

Adopt watchful monitoring for CBL-associated JMML that may follow an indolent or self-limiting course, reserving chemotherapy and haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation for progressive or aggressive disease
Assess and monitor cardiac involvement with echocardiography, though it is often milder than in classic Noonan syndrome
Monitor growth with endocrine assessment of short stature
Provide neurodevelopmental assessment and support for delay
Remain alert to RAS-pathway complications such as vasculitis
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant germline CBL RASopathy, with testing of relatives
Coordinate care through clinical genetics and paediatric haemato-oncology
